scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Sega originated in the 18th century among enslaved populations in the Indian Ocean.
It is a fusion of African and Malagasy rhythms with European folk dance elements like the polka, waltz, and quadrille.
Historically, it was performed in private and often faced opposition from colonial authorities and the Catholic Church due to its perceived sensuality.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Sega is a social and community-building art form.
Historically, it was used for dirges, exorcisms, and protest (Santé engagé).
It serves as a symbol of cultural identity and resilience, transcending social and ethnic barriers in modern society.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The dance is performed with the feet remaining in constant contact with the ground.
Dancers move their hips and waist in fluid, circular motions.
Partners interact in a playful game where the woman leads the movement and the man attempts to follow or anticipate her direction.
Watch for Hip Rotation.

Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Couples or groups moving in circular paths.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Traditional music relies on the ravanne (goatskin drum), maravanne (rattle), triangle, and bobre (bow).
Modern ensembles may include electric guitars, keyboards, and bass.
Listen for the ravanne, maravanne, triangle, bobre.
The pulse is 6/8.
A percussive, drum-heavy sound driven by the deep resonance of the ravanne and the metallic shimmer of the triangle, often featuring call-and-response vocals.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Women traditionally wear large, colorful circular skirts and tops that bare the midriff to accentuate hip movements.
Men wear colorful shirts, shorts, and straw hats.
Performances occur in private family settings, public community events, and formal festivals.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ti Frère, a Mauritian artist, is credited with bringing sega into the public sphere in the 1960s.
Other key figures include Serge Lebrasse, Claudio Veeraragoo, and Kaya, the pioneer of the seggae fusion genre.
Mauritius features 'Sega Tipik'; Rodrigues is known for the fast-paced 'Sega Tambour' and 'Segakordeon'; Réunion shares roots with the distinct but related 'Maloya'; the Seychelles practice 'Moutia'.
Sega shares historical links with the Maloya of Réunion and is influenced by African, Malagasy, and European dance traditions.
